name: Vase designed by Carl-Harry Stålhane for Rörstrand
description:
This stoneware vase by Carl-Harry Stålhane is defined by its tall, slender proportions and quietly tapered cylindrical form. Its restrained expression is characteristic of Stålhane’s approach to stoneware, where proportion, material and glaze were allowed to speak for themselves.

Carl-Harry Stålhane (1920–1990) was one of Sweden’s leading ceramicists of the twentieth century and an important figure in Rörstrand’s artistic development. He joined the factory as a decorator before studying sculpture at Konstfack, later becoming one of its most influential designers. Founded in 1726, Rörstrand is one of Europe’s oldest porcelain manufacturers and played a central role in the development of Swedish ceramics, particularly during the 20th century.

Signed

name: Globe vase designed by Mari Simmulson for Uppsala-Ekeby
description:
This large globe vase by Mari Simmulson is a unique work in earthenware, distinguished by its generous spherical form and bold painted decoration. A deep, glossy ground is articulated with broad vertical bands in black and rich blue, creating a strong rhythm across the curved surface. The contrast between the dark glaze and cooler blue tones gives the vase considerable depth, while the high-gloss finish catches and reflects light, enhancing its sculptural, almost jewel-like presence.

Mari Simmulson was one of the most versatile and important designers associated with Upsala-Ekeby. Born in 1911, she arrived in Sweden from Estonia in 1944 and initially worked at Gustavsberg before joining Upsala-Ekeby in 1949, where she remained for more than two decades. Her practice encompassed painting, sculpture, textiles, illustration and ceramics, and she developed more than 200 ceramic series during her time at the factory.

Signed

name: Casserole dish designed by Karin Björquist for Gustavsberg
description:
Designed by Karin Björquist for Gustavsberg in 1962, this stoneware dish combines robust functionality with the restrained material sensibility characteristic of Swedish mid-century ceramics. Its broad cylindrical body is flanked by two generously proportioned loop handles and fitted with a gently domed lid, creating a compact and well-balanced silhouette.

The surface is covered in a deep, glossy brown glaze. Depending on the light, the colour shifts from near-black and deep charcoal to warmer reddish-brown and amber tones, particularly around the handles, rim and areas where the glaze thins.

Karin Björquist was one of the leading figures in twentieth-century Swedish ceramics. She joined Gustavsberg in 1950 after being encouraged by the factory’s artistic director Wilhelm Kåge, and subsequently worked within the faience department under Stig Lindberg. By the early 1950s she had been given her own studio, and her first table service entered production in 1952. Her long association with Gustavsberg culminated in her appointment as the company’s first female artistic director in 1981.

Signed

name: Bowl designed by Carl-Harry Stålhane for Rörstrand
description:
This unique stoneware bowl by Carl-Harry Stålhane is a refined example of Swedish studio ceramics, combining a quietly balanced form with a richly nuanced glaze. Its simplicity places particular emphasis on the surface, where a deep sienna-brown glaze develops subtle tonal variations across the rounded body before breaking into a softly frosted, pale edge around the rim.

The bowl belongs to Stålhane’s tradition of unikat, or unique works conceived as individual art objects rather than serially produced ceramics. For Stålhane, these pieces were the result of a highly controlled and personal process. Even when he did not carry out every stage himself, he remained closely involved in the shaping, throwing and glazing, supervising the work to ensure that each object met his standards. This rigorous approach gives his unique stoneware a particular significance within his wider production.

Carl-Harry Stålhane was one of Sweden’s most important twentieth-century ceramicists and a central figure in Rörstrand’s artistic production. Beginning at the factory as a decorator, he later studied sculpture at Konstfack and developed a highly individual approach to stoneware based on controlled proportions, experimental glazes and an intimate understanding of the material.

Unique. Signed.

name: Vase designed by Bente Hansen
description:
A porcelain vase designed by Bente Hansen in Denmark in 2000, signed and dated on the base with the monogram BH 2000 and marked “68”. The vase has an organic oval body with a softly flattened base and an angled opening, combining a matte white unglazed exterior with a glossy black-glazed interior. The vase belongs to Hansen’s more reduced studio work, where the emphasis moves away from applied pattern and towards form and monochrome contrast.

Bente Hansen is a Danish ceramic artist working in porcelain and stoneware. For several decades she has produced both functional and sculptural ceramics from her workshop, with a practice rooted in wheel-thrown forms, and a strong understanding of proportion. Her work has ranged from richly patterned pieces to more minimal monochrome vessels, reflecting a continued interest in the relationship between shape, decoration and material.

Signed

name: Vase 'Crowd'Designed by Mårten MedboSweden, 2012
description: A vase from the “Crowd” series designed by Mårten Medbo in Sweden, formed as a dense cluster of rounded, egg-like volumes gathered (9061)

name: Vase 'Unic' designed by Gunnar Nylund for ALP Lidköping
description:
This ‘Unic’ stoneware vase by Gunnar Nylund for ALP Lidköping is a one-off piece, created as an individual work rather than as part of a standard production series. The ‘Unic’ designation was reserved for unique examples, giving each vase its own distinct character and making works from the series particularly interesting within Nylund’s wider ceramic production. The vase has a softly rounded body, a slightly narrowing upper section and a low foot ring. The surface is finished in a dark brown, iron-rich glaze with a matte to semi-matte character, shifting subtly between black, brown and warmer undertones as it catches the light.

AB Lidköpings Porslinsfabrik, often abbreviated ALP, was an important Swedish porcelain manufacturer. In 1932, the company became connected with Rörstrand, and works designed under Rörstrand’s artistic direction were also produced at the Lidköping facilities. Pieces bearing the ALP Lidköping mark belong to this transitional period before the mark was later replaced by the Rörstrand name, giving them a distinct place within Swedish ceramic production.

Gunnar Nylund (1904–1997) was one of the leading figures in twentieth-century Swedish ceramics. He is closely associated with Rörstrand, where he served as artistic director from the 1930s to the 1950s. His work is recognised for its organic forms, subtle asymmetry and richly developed glazes, ranging from vessels and bowls to animal figures and architectural ceramics. Through this balance of form, material and firing technique, Nylund helped define the artistic direction of modern Swedish stoneware.

Stamped

name: Bowl 'AXK Series' designed by Gunnar Nylund for Rörstrand
description:
A stoneware bowl from the AXK series, designed by Gunnar Nylund for Rörstrand in Sweden in 1957, with an open, softly irregular form and a gently undulating rim.

The glaze gives the bowl its principal character. Brown and black tones run through the blue field in a hare’s-fur effect, created as the feldspar glaze moved during firing. This process gives each example an individual surface, with variations in pooling, streaking and depth.

Gunnar Nylund (1904–1997) was one of the leading figures in twentieth-century Swedish ceramics. He is closely associated with Rörstrand, where he served as artistic director from the 1930s to the 1950s. His work is recognised for its organic forms, subtle asymmetry and richly developed glazes, ranging from vessels and bowls to animal figures and architectural ceramics. Through this balance of form, material and firing technique, Nylund helped define the artistic direction of modern Swedish stoneware.

Signed

name: Bowl designed by Brita Mellander-Jungerman
description:
This octagonal stoneware bowl was designed by Brita Mellander-Jungerman in Sweden, with a faceted exterior and a white-glazed interior. The low, open form is defined by sharply angled planes that give the bowl a geometric profile, while the contrast between the warm exterior glaze and the light interior emphasises its architectural construction. The piece is signed.

Brita Mellander-Jungerman was a Swedish ceramic artist and designer educated at Konstfack in Stockholm between 1953 and 1957. She later worked for Karlskrona Porcelain Factory, where she introduced more colourful, abstract and geometric decoration into the company’s production. Her work ranged from domestic porcelain to individual studio pieces, combining industrial design with a personal ceramic language.

Mellander-Jungerman also travelled widely and studied ceramic traditions beyond Sweden, including in Japan. Her work has been shown internationally and is represented in Swedish museum collections, where she is recognised as part of the development of Swedish modern ceramics.

Unique

name: Egg sculpture designed by Vincent Nilsson for Höganäs
description:
An egg-shaped stoneware sculpture designed by Vincent Nilsson for Höganäs in Sweden, with a rounded organic form and a flowing glaze in cream and green tones. The egg was one of Nilsson’s recurring sculptural motifs, alongside other natural forms such as fruit. The sculpture is signed and marked Höganäs underneath.

Vincent Nilsson was a Swedish ceramic artist closely associated with the Höganäs region in southern Sweden, an area long known for its clay traditions and studio pottery. He was the son of the ceramicist Henning Nilsson and trained within that environment from an early age, developing a strong knowledge of glaze chemistry and firing techniques. His work is particularly noted for its experimental surfaces and richly modulated glazes, which give even reduced sculptural forms a strong visual presence.

Signed

name: VesselDesigned by Sandra DavolioDenmark, 2026
description: Signed porcelain vessel by Sandra Davolio, Denmark, 2026 - layered, undulating forms inspired by ancient Mediterranean ceramics. Height 15 cm.

name: A set of 27 piece tableware 'Pencil' designed by Stig Lindberg for Gustavsberg
description:
0This 27-piece tableware set from the ‘Pencil’ series by Stig Lindberg reflects the restrained elegance that became central to Scandinavian table design during the post-war period. Executed in fine bone china, the service is decorated with delicate black linear motifs that resemble quick pencil strokes drawn across the white surface. The set consists of eleven dinner plates, twelve starter plates and four bowls.

‘Pencil’ emerged during a period when Swedish design strongly embraced the idea of creating beautiful objects for ordinary life, where mass-produced domestic wares were expected to combine practicality with artistic quality. The series remains one of the clearest examples of this philosophy.

Stig Lindberg (1916–1982) was one of Sweden’s most influential ceramicists and designers of the twentieth century. During his long association with Gustavsberg, he created ceramics, textiles and industrial designs distinguished by their imaginative forms and highly individual visual language. His work helped define the character of post-war Scandinavian design and continues to be celebrated for balancing artistic experimentation with functional everyday use.

Stamped

name: Vase 'Model 385' designed by Vicke Lindstrand for Uppsala Ekeby
description:
This glazed earthenware vase designed by Vicke Lindstrand for Uppsala-Ekeby. The vase is decorated in light yellow and brown glazes, with incised female figures set against a mottled ceramic surface. Signed “Vicke” at the base and stamped underneath “Ekeby 385 V.L”.

The decoration is executed using a sgraffito technique, in which the contours of the figures are incised directly into the clay body before firing. This gives the line work a physical presence within the surface, rather than appearing only as painted decoration.

Vicke Lindstrand (1904–1983) was one of Sweden’s most influential designers of the twentieth century, working across glass, ceramics, textiles and industrial design. He first became known for his work at Orrefors, where he contributed to the development of Graal glass during the 1920s and 1930s. In 1942, Lindstrand joined Uppsala-Ekeby, where he shifted his focus to ceramics and introduced a more modern, graphic sensibility to the company’s production. His ceramic works from this period often combine hand-drawn decoration with simplified forms, frequently depicting figures, animals and mythological or theatrical subjects.

Signed

name: Vase designed by Hans Vangsø
description:
This vase designed by Hans Vangsø has a thick white glaze and a heavily textured surface, with cratered openings, small dark inclusions and areas where the glaze has fused closely with the clay body, giving the piece a distinctly geological character. To achieve these alive, bubbling surfaces, Vangsø pours glazes thickly and uses unconventional combustible materials such as seaweed, salt, metals and newspaper during the firing process. The vase is monogrammed with Vangsø’s signature mark.

The compact, rounded form recalls East Asian ceramic traditions, particularly moon jars and tea vessels, while the treatment remains closely tied to Danish studio pottery. Vangsø’s work is shaped by the firing process, where glaze, clay and kiln atmosphere interact at high temperatures to produce surfaces that cannot be fully controlled.

Hans Vangsø studied at the Jutland Academy of Fine Arts from 1972 to 1976 and worked closely with Gutte Eriksen, one of the central figures in modern Danish studio ceramics. His practice continues the robust, material-focused tradition of Danish stoneware, with an emphasis on firing, surface and the individual character of each vessel.

Monogrammed

name: Vase designed by Berndt Friberg for Gustavsberg
description:
Berndt Friberg was one of the most accomplished Swedish ceramicists of the 20th century, renowned for his exceptional glazes and forms. Unlike many of his contemporaries, Friberg personally threw and glazed every piece he created, earning him a reputation for unparalleled craftsmanship. His mastery of the rabbit’s fur glaze technique, achieved by mouth-spraying layers of differently coloured glazes, resulted in a striking variety of hues that collectors highly prize. During his lifetime, Friberg enjoyed great success, with even the King of Sweden, an avid ceramics collector, previewing his exhibitions to select pieces before the public.

Friberg’s work evolved over time, with his early matte glazes giving way to shinier finishes from the late 1950s, often featuring striking geometric patterns. His creations ranged from tiny miniatures, some no larger than a few centimetres, to large floor vases, each meticulously crafted with a small foot ring characteristic of his style. A perfectionist, Friberg ensured that his vessels were flawless, carefully avoiding dried glaze droplets on the brown foot rings that became a hallmark of his work.

For nearly fifty years, Friberg worked at Gustavsberg, Sweden’s most prestigious porcelain company, established in 1826. He began as a thrower for Wilhelm Kåge in 1934 and later collaborated with Stig Lindberg while developing his own signature style, influenced by traditional Asian pottery. His elegant designs, combined with his technical prowess, solidified his legacy as a master of Swedish ceramics.

Signed
material: Stoneware, hare's fur glaze in dove blue

name: Vase designed by Dagmar Norell
description:
This stoneware vase/sculpture was made by Dagmar Norell in her own workshop in Spånga during the 1980s. Formed in unglazed white clay, the piece has the abstracted shape of a female torso, with broad shoulders, a narrowed neck and softly modelled volume. The absence of glaze gives the surface a quiet, tactile quality, allowing subtle variations in the clay and the shadows across the form to become central to the work.

Norell’s later ceramics are closely associated with this raw, pale material and with forms shaped through touch rather than sight. Having lost her eyesight earlier in life, she developed a sculptural language based on tactile memory, proportion and physical sensitivity.

Dagmar Norell was originally trained as a medical doctor and psychiatrist before turning to ceramics after losing her sight in the 1950s. She established her own workshop in Spånga and made her artistic debut in Stockholm in 1969. Her work is represented in major Swedish collections, including Nationalmuseum in Stockholm and the Röhsska Museum in Gothenburg.

Signed DN

name: Bowl designed by Cecilia Kraitz
description:
This Swedish ceramic bowl by Cecilia Kraitz is a striking example of Scandinavian ceramics, where material, process, and surface come together in a highly expressive composition. The deep black ground is punctuated by irregular turquoise fields, each defined by a fine network of crackle lines. This deliberate crackle effect, known as kannyū, is created through the controlled tension between glaze and clay during cooling.

Kraitz often works with techniques related to the Raku tradition, where rapid cooling plays a central role in shaping the final appearance. In this process, the glaze contracts and fractures, while smoke penetrates the fine cracks and settles into the surface, making each line visible and permanent. This approach reflects a sensitivity to the Japanese philosophy of wabi-sabi, where irregularity, imperfection and the marks of process are understood as integral to beauty.

Cecilia Kraitz, born in 1964, was raised in close proximity to clay as the daughter of ceramicists Ulla and Gustav Kraitz. Her work builds on this foundation while developing a distinct language of her own, centred on stoneware forms and complex glaze techniques.

Signed

name: Ceramic planter designed by Margareta Wibom for Bo Fajans
description:
This ceramic planter by Margareta (Maggie) Wibom is defined by its sculptural relief of stylised vines and leaves, wrapping rhythmically around the body. Executed in chamotted stoneware, the material provides both durability and a subtle texture beneath the glaze. The combination of robust construction and expressive surface treatment reflects the transition from Swedish Grace to early modernism, where ornament is integrated into form.

Produced by Bo Fajans in Gävle, a factory known for its high-quality artistic ceramics, the planter belongs to a period of notable creativity during the interwar years. Margareta Wibom (1899–1961) was a sculptor and ceramicist who contributed to renewing Swedish ceramic design in the 1920s and 1930s. Among the first women to establish herself in the field, her work is characterised by a strong sense of form and an interest in relief decoration rooted in both tradition and modern expression.

Signed

name: 'Karneval' vase designed by Stig Lindberg for Gustavsberg
description:
Designed by Stig Lindberg for Gustavsberg, the Karneval vase belongs to one of the most celebrated ceramic series of Swedish post-war design. Produced between 1958 and 1962, the series comprised a wide range of vases and platters, each decorated with playful, stylised motifs that exemplify Lindberg’s distinctive visual language.

The vase is made in faience and decorated with a rhythmic arrangement of graphic forms that move around the cylindrical body. The motifs were first applied as black outlines and then carefully coloured by hand, resulting in subtle variations from piece to piece. Much of the vitality of the Karneval series comes from this process, and from the contribution of skilled painters such as Karin Gustavsson, whose hand-painted colour work gives each example its individual character and depth.

Karneval reflects Lindberg’s belief that everyday objects could be both functional and imaginative. Created during the era of the Swedish Folkhemmet, the series aligned with the ideal of making well-designed, artistically ambitious objects accessible for daily life. Stig Lindberg, who served as artistic director at Gustavsberg from 1949, played a decisive role in shaping modern Swedish ceramics, and the Karneval series remains a vivid illustration of his ability to combine humour, craftsmanship and modern form in a way that continues to feel fresh and engaging.

Signed

name: Vase/candlestick 'Snurran' by Stig Lindberg for Gustavsberg
description:
Stig Lindberg’s “Snurran” vases belong to a limited and timeless series. The name “Snurran” refers to the vase’s ability to be turned, allowing the piece to function in multiple ways. Depending on its orientation, it can serve as two vases with a central candle holder, or alternatively as two candle holders with a single vase.

Lindberg’s pieces captured the spirit of the times; they are whimsical, playful, and optimistic. Some of his pieces are fantastically patterned, and he frequently combined abstract patterns with motifs from nature.

Stig Lindberg was one of the most influential Swedish ceramic designers of the post-war period. He worked across unique art pieces and serial production, becoming particularly associated with faience and utilitarian wares. In 1949, he was appointed artistic director at Gustavsberg, the historic Swedish porcelain manufacturer founded in 1826, where he had earlier worked as an assistant to Wilhelm Kåge. Trained initially as a painter, Lindberg brought a strong graphic sensibility to ceramics, contributing to the renewal of tin-glazed faience and establishing a body of work defined by clarity, and technical confidence.

Signed with Studiohånden, Sweden, 26.III

name: Plate designed by Tyra Lundgren for Rörstrand
description:
This elegant stoneware dish designed by Tyra Lundgren for Rörstrand is a distinguished example of early Nordic mid century design in ceramics. Executed in high-fired stoneware, the surface carries a softly modulated blue underglaze and features a motif of a woman integrated into the form.

The impressed Rörstrand signature with date underline the dish’s authentic place in Rörstrand’s artistic production of the period. Lundgren (1897–1979) worked as a designer at Rörstrand during the late 1920s and early 1930s, at a time when the factory was exploring more sculptural and modern approaches within its ceramic output.

Signed TL Rörstrand 1930

name: Vase designed by Allan Ebeling
description:
This sculptural terracotta vase by Allan Ebeling is a striking example of his experimental approach to Swedish ceramics in the mid-20th century. Handbuilt in Torshälla, the piece has a triangular footprint, with each vertical face animated by a column of rounded protrusions that swell rhythmically along the height of the vessel. The relief modelling gives the form a strong architectural presence while the repeated bulges create a dynamic play of light and shadow across the matte, unglazed surface.

The warm, natural tone of the earthenware reveals subtle traces of the hand, underscoring Ebeling’s background as both sculptor and ceramic artist. Rather than relying on colour or glaze, he allows volume, proportion and texture to carry the expression, aligning this vase with the modernist interest in pure form. Signed “AE” and standing over 45 cm high, it functions as both container and autonomous sculpture, reflecting the freedom and individuality that define Allan Ebeling’s contribution to Swedish studio ceramics.

name: Bowl designed by Rolf Palm
description:
This ceramic bowl by Swedish studio potter Rolf Palm exemplifies the refined artistry of Scandinavian ceramic design in the mid-20th century. Hand-thrown and signed by the artist, the piece displays Palm’s signature earthy glaze palette, a natural fusion of muted tones, speckled surfaces, and subtle variations that highlight the handmade process.

The softly rounded forms and tactile finishes reflect Palm’s deep connection to the material and his mastery of traditional stoneware techniques, developed over decades at his studio in Mölle, Sweden. His work, often celebrated for its quiet strength and organic beauty, bridges functionality and sculpture with a distinctly Nordic sensibility.

name: Sculpture 'Springare' designed by Stig Lindberg for Gustavsberg
description:
The “Springare” by Stig Lindberg is a refined ceramic sculpture from Sweden’s mid‑20th‑century design era. Crafted in the 1950s for the Gustavsberg Porcelain Factory, this piece interprets the theme of a horse in a sculptural form that balances simplicity and expression. With its softly rounded body, spindly legs and minimal head, the figure embodies Lindberg’s characteristic blend of humour, elegance and craft. This version features a light glaze with subtle painted and incised detailing, offering both visual calm and textural interest.

Lindberg’s work at Gustavsberg and his broader career as a designer and educator mark him as one of the most versatile and influential voices in Swedish design history.

name: Dragon sculpture designed by Wilhelm Kåge for Gustavsberg
description:
Wilhelm Kåge's dragon sculptures, crafted at Gustavsberg during the late 1930s to 1950s, exemplify his innovative approach to ceramic art. The sculpture showcase a blend of whimsical design and Kåge’s craftmanship. Kåge's dragon sculptures are characterized by their stylized forms, featuring exaggerated features such as pronounced eyes, curled tails, and textured bodies all seen in this piece.

Dragons offered Kåge a departure from the functionalist ideals that had dominated much of his earlier career. These creatures provided a canvas for sculptural and expressive freedom and blending Kåge’s humour and fantasy. The dragons, often affectionately referred to as drakvalpar (dragon puppies), possess a charm and personality that contrast with the restrained aesthetics of his tableware.

name: Vase 'Farsta' designed by Wilhelm Kåge for Gustavsbergs Studio
description:
The Farsta series by Wilhelm Kåge, produced between 1930 and 1960 at the Gustavsberg studio is one of his most exclusive and celebrated series. Characterised by sculptural forms and incised geometric patterns, the pieces are made from reddish-brown stoneware, with thick glazes that create striking colour effects. Each object is handmade and their unique shapes range from vases and bowls to urns, sculptures and wall plaques. The high iron content of the clay, sourced from Höganäs in southern Sweden, lends the pieces their signature dark colour, while Kåge’s skillful use of metal oxides during the glazing process results in their renowned visual impact.

Named after the Farstalandet region surrounding the Gustavsberg factory, the Farsta series was first presented at the 1930 Stockholm Exhibition, where it garnered significant attention. Kåge’s dedication to the series is evident in his own words: “Farsta has been my only true uncompromising work at Gustavsberg.”

Wilhelm Kåge (1889–1960) was a groundbreaking Swedish ceramic designer and painter, renowned for his innovations in ceramic design. Trained as a painter in Paris, Kåge was brought to Gustavsberg to rejuvenate and modernise the artistic tradition of the pottery company. Kåge served as the artistic director at Gustavsberg from 1917 to 1949 and played a crucial role in shaping the modern ceramic movement in Sweden.

name: Vase model 11181 'Manhattan' designed by Berit Ternell, Upsala-Ekeby
description:
The Manhattan series is a notable collection of ceramic pieces designed by Swedish artist Berit Ternell for Upsala-Ekeby. This series is characterized by its modernist aesthetic, featuring clean lines and geometric form: a shape reminiscent of New York’s towering skyline.

Berit Ternell (born 1929) is a distinguished Swedish ceramic artist and designer, renowned for her significant contributions to mid-20th-century Scandinavian ceramics.

name: Vase 'Surrea' by Wilhelm Kåge for Gustavsberg
description:
Wilhelm Kåge’s Surrea series, launched in 1940, reflects his forward-thinking approach to ceramic art. Comprising mainly vases and bowls in stoneware, the series is known for its asymmetrical, disrupted forms and soft white Carrara glaze. Many pieces appear as if sliced and reassembled, evoking both Cubist geometry and surrealist detachment.

Production was exceptionally limited, owing to the technical challenges of assembling the segmented forms without causing firing cracks. The precision this required highlights Kåge’s mastery of the medium.

Born in 1889, Kåge served as artistic director at Gustavsberg from 1917 to 1949, where he played a central role in redefining Swedish design. From refined everyday tableware to more radical works like Surrea, his practice consistently explored the intersection of function and artistic vision. Deeply rooted in modernist ideals, his legacy continues to shape the narrative of 20th-century Scandinavian design.

description:
The vibrant turquoise-to-deep-blue hue reflects a high level of craftsmanship, a hallmark of Berndt Friberg's work. This attention to detail is further evident in the slight lifting at the base, which reveals unglazed stoneware—a classic feature of his pieces.

Berndt Friberg (1899–1981) was one of Sweden’s most revered ceramic artists, celebrated for his delicately thrown stoneware and masterful glazes. Working for Gustavsberg, a major Swedish porcelain and ceramics manufacturer, he developed an extraordinary precision in both form and surface treatment, elevating his work to an art form.

name: Vase designed by Berndt Friberg, Gustavsbergs Studio
description:
This vase showcases a soft ochre-yellow glaze with subtle tonal variations that enhance its depth and texture. The silky matte finish, a hallmark of Berndt Friberg’s work, reflects his meticulous glazing techniques and precise firing process. The gentle swirling effect at the base adds a sense of movement, highlighting his mastery of form and surface.

Berndt Friberg (1899–1981) was a renowned Swedish ceramicist known for his expertly thrown stoneware and refined glazes. During his time at Gustavsberg, he perfected his craft, achieving an exceptional balance of elegance and technical precision.

name: Bowl designed by Vicke Lindstrand for Upsala Ekeby
description:
This ceramic plate by Vicke Lindstrand (1904–1983) showcases his unique approach to form and decoration, seamlessly blending figuration with expressive, painterly techniques.

A highly influential Swedish designer, Lindstrand made significant contributions to both glass and ceramics. After pioneering the development of Graal glass at Orrefors in the 1920s and 1930s, he transitioned to Upsala-Ekeby in 1942, shifting his focus to ceramics. During this period, he introduced a modernist sensibility to Swedish pottery, creating decorative ceramics with hand-painted designs, often featuring stylized figures—exemplified beautifully in this piece.

name: Vase designed by Gunnar Nylund, Rörstrand
description:
This vase exemplifies Gunnar Nylund’s mid-century approach to ceramics, where glazes were integral to creating depth and texture, enhancing the simplicity of his refined forms. The rich ochre and deep red hues blend seamlessly across the surface, creating a soft, feathered effect that showcases Nylund’s mastery of glaze application. Resting on a small, subtly raised foot, the vase appears to hover lightly, a hallmark of Nylund’s work that heightens its sense of refinement.

Gunnar Nylund (1904–1997) was a pioneering Swedish ceramicist and designer, best known for his work at Rörstrand, where he served as artistic director from the 1930s to the 1950s. His ceramics are characterised by organic, sculptural forms, richly textured glazes, and a modernist aesthetic that blends functionality with artistic expression.

name: Vase designed by Carl-Harry Stålhane, Rörstrand
description:
This vase embodies Carl-Harry Stålhane’s refined approach to form and glazing, where subtle variations in tone and texture bring depth to its elegantly simple silhouette. Known for his technical precision, Stålhane perfected the balance between sculptural presence and functional design, often working with soft, muted glazes that highlight the natural beauty of the ceramic surface. White glazing was a favourite among designers like Stålhane for its ability to highlight form and texture without distraction.

Carl-Harry Stålhane (1920–1990) was one of Sweden’s most influential ceramicists and designers, known for his refined forms, innovative glazing techniques, and deep influence on Scandinavian modernism. His career at Rörstrand, one of Sweden’s most prestigious ceramics manufacturers, spanned several decades, during which he shaped the company’s artistic direction and established himself as a leading figure in Swedish design.

description:
This model is characterized by its elegant, elongated form and distinctive "hare's fur" glaze—a reddish-brown finish that darkens near the base. The SYA vases are part of Stålhane's "Alphabet" series, where each model was assigned a unique combination of letters, such as SYA, SYB, and SYE. The SYA model, with its refined silhouette and rich glaze, exemplifies Stålhane's contribution to mid-century Scandinavian design.

Carl-Harry Stålhane (1920–1990) was one of Sweden’s most significant ceramicists, shaping the artistic direction of Rörstrand from the 1940s through the 1970s. He began his career as a decorator before becoming the company’s artistic director, developing a signature style that balanced modernist simplicity with an appreciation for traditional craftsmanship.

Before becoming one of Sweden’s most renowned ceramicists, he actually started out as a decorator at Rörstrand in the 1930s, hand-painting designs onto pottery. His artistic career took a major turn when he studied sculpture at Konstfack and later became Rörstrand’s leading designer, creating elegant stoneware pieces that are now highly collectible.

name: Sculpture alligator retailed by Svenskt Tenn
description:
This hand-modelled terracotta sculpture depicts an alligator rendered in a naturalistic form. The figure is modelled fully in the round, with individually shaped scales, limbs, and tail, and finished with a glossy green-brown glaze. The irregularities in the modelling and glaze indicate studio or workshop production rather than moulded manufacture.

The sculpture was made in Italy during the 1950s, a period when Italian ceramic workshops produced a wide range of decorative animal figures for export. Such objects were frequently retailed by Northern European design firms, including Svenskt Tenn in Stockholm, which was known for its curated selection of handcrafted decorative pieces alongside modern furniture and interiors.

Animal sculptures in ceramic and metal formed a recurring category in Svenskt Tenn’s assortment during the mid-20th century, valued for their tactile qualities and sculptural presence. The present example reflects this approach, combining traditional terracotta techniques with a subject chosen for decorative use in domestic interiors. The maker is unknown, which is typical for workshop-produced ceramics of this period.

name: Lidded urn designed by Wilhelm Kåge, Gustavsberg, Farsta
description:
The Farsta series by Wilhelm Kåge, produced between 1930 and 1960 at the Gustavsberg studio is one of his most exclusive and celebrated series. Characterised by sculptural forms and incised geometric patterns, the pieces are made from reddish-brown stoneware, with thick glazes that create striking colour effects. Each object is handmade and their unique shapes range from vases and bowls to urns, sculptures and wall plaques. The high iron content of the clay, sourced from Höganäs in southern Sweden, lends the pieces their signature dark colour, while Kåge’s skillful use of metal oxides during the glazing process results in their renowned visual impact.

Named after the Farstalandet region surrounding the Gustavsberg factory, the Farsta series was first presented at the 1930 Stockholm Exhibition, where it garnered significant attention. Kåge’s dedication to the series is evident in his own words: “Farsta has been my only true uncompromising work at Gustavsberg.”

Wilhelm Kåge (1889–1960) was a groundbreaking Swedish ceramic designer and painter, renowned for his innovations in ceramic design. Trained as a painter in Paris, Kåge was brought to Gustavsberg to rejuvenate and modernise the artistic tradition of the pottery company. Kåge served as the artistic director at Gustavsberg from 1917 to 1949 and played a crucial role in shaping the modern ceramic movement in Sweden.

Signed.

name: Vase by Berndt Friberg for Gustavsberg
description:
Berndt Friberg was one of the most accomplished Swedish ceramicists of the 20th century, renowned for his exceptional glazes and forms. Unlike many of his contemporaries, Friberg personally threw and glazed every piece he created, earning him a reputation for unparalleled craftsmanship. His mastery of the rabbit’s fur glaze technique, achieved by mouth-spraying layers of differently coloured glazes, resulted in a striking variety of hues that collectors highly prize. During his lifetime, Friberg enjoyed great success, with even the King of Sweden, an avid ceramics collector, previewing his exhibitions to select pieces before the public. Friberg’s work evolved over time, with his early matte glazes giving way to shinier finishes from the late 1950s, often featuring striking geometric patterns. His creations ranged from tiny miniatures, some no larger than a few centimetres, to large floor vases, each meticulously crafted with a small foot ring characteristic of his style. A perfectionist, Friberg ensured that his vessels were flawless, carefully avoiding dried glaze droplets on the brown foot rings that became a hallmark of his work. For nearly fifty years, Friberg worked at Gustavsberg, Sweden’s most prestigious porcelain company, established in 1826. He began as a thrower for Wilhelm Kåge in 1934 and later collaborated with Stig Lindberg while developing his own signature style, influenced by traditional Asian pottery. His elegant designs, combined with his technical prowess, solidified his legacy as a master of Swedish ceramics.

Signed.

In the early stages of his career, Carlsson worked under the mentorship of Gunnar Nylund at Rörstrand. In 1955 he starting working at IFÖ Verken in Bromölla, where he assumed the role of chief designer and specialised in creating chamotte garden urns. He went on to work for Jie Gantofta in the late 1960s.

By the mid-1970s, Carlsson established his own studio in Nyhamnsläge. This studio became a creative hub where he crafted a variety of unique items, including ceramics, nail sculptures, and wall art. His craft extended to numerous public works and decorative projects.

name: Sculpture by Per Hammarström
description:
Per Hammarström is one of Sweden’s most highly regarded ceramicists. Per’s work doesn’t conform to the Swedish style of simplicity; instead he loves colour and texture, and exploring the multi-faceted function of ceramics. Per began his training at the Gustavsbergs Porcelain Studio in 1978, which is sadly no longer in existence. In 1984 he opened his own studio in Strängnäs, and has worked in this manner ever since.

Per’s work is characterised by organic forms and his own distinctive glazes, often in bright colours and strong contrasts. His work is unique, each piece starting out as a roughly thrown form, which is worked and transformed into bowls that are characterised by their delicacy and translucency. The organic form is embodied in the textured ceramics of Per. His works are either made from stoneware or porcelain.

The inspiration of much of his work is the sea, but he also draws from flora and fauna; and the changing of the seasons. The undulating colours of the sea, sky and land manifest themselves in his delicately crafted and vividly coloured ceramics. Through elaborate dining-ware and ceramic ornaments, Per’s work evokes the wonders of the world, both past, present, and imagined.

Per has exhibited throughout Sweden, including at the Royal Palace in Stockholm, in 2015; as well as at Ceramic’s Biennale in Cairo, Egypt 1996.

Signed.

name: Vase by Kyllikki Salmenhaara for Arabia
description:
Salmenhaara began to study at the Department of Ceramics of the Central School of Applied Arts under Elsa Elenius. Her studies were interrupted during the Second World War when Salmenhaara served in a women's auxiliary capacity. She graduated in 1943 and went on to work for three years at the Kauklahti glassworks near Helsinki. Before entering the service of the Arabia factory, Salmenhaara spent a trainee period in Nathalie Grebs's studio in Denmark and worked in Sakari Vapaavuori's studio in Finland.

Kyllikki Salmenhaara worked as a member of Arabia team from 1947 until 1961.Together with other designers of the Arabia factory's Art Department, Salmenhaara participated in numerous int' exhibitions and was often awarded prizes, particularly at the Milan Triennials of 1951-1960. She received the Pro Finlandia medal in 1961. In the autumn of 1963, after Elsa Elenius became ill, Salmenhaara was appointed to carry on the teaching of ceramics at the Ateneum in Helsinki. One of the goals of that period was to bring teaching closer to professional practices and the needs of industry. Salmenhaara began to systematically develop material studies and the teaching of small-scale production methods. Kyllikki Salmenhaara was appointed to Finland's first post as artist professor in the field of design and applied art from 1970 to 1973. She died of cancer in 1981, but her influence has been passed on to later generations of ceramists.

name: Bowl 'Veckla' designed by Stig Lindberg for Gustavsberg
description:
Stig Lindberg’s “Veckla” vases and bowls belong to a series produced in limited numbers. Lindberg frequently reinterpreted natural occurrences with organic forms; this piece resembles a coral or tree branch. “Veckla” means “folded”, which refers to the shape.

These stoneware sculptures were glazed with matte white Carrara glaze and manufactured by Gustavsberg from the late 1940s until the 1950s.

Stig Lindberg was one of the most influential Swedish ceramics designers of the post-war years. His designs include individual art pieces as well as decorative production wares, exemplified by many faience designs and utilitarian wares.

In 1949, Lindberg became the artistic director at Gustavsberg, the famous Swedish porcelain company that originated in 1826. He had begun his career as an assistant to Wilhelm Kåge at Gustavsberg. Kåge had discovered the young Lindberg who, just like Kåge himself, was initially a painter.
